children: The global rally in all things AI (artificial intelligence) has convinced many Indian investors that foreign stocks offer an easy route to riches. In the last two years, they’ve raked in big money from casual bets on South Korean and Taiwanese indices, semiconductor and memory names like SK hynix and Taiwan Semiconductor and hyper-scaler plays such as Nvidia, Meta or Alphabet.

However, the global AI trade is now developing cracks. Recent events have also shown that companies listed in other markets are as liable to disruption from macro factors, slowdown fears and CEO misdemeanor, as Indian companies are. In fact, investing in foreign stocks is infinitely more complicated than your home market, because there are many additional risks to consider. Here are some factors to run a check on.
Growth rate

Despite all the flak it has been getting, India is among the fastest-growing large economies in the world, consistently managing real GDP growth of 7 per cent plus and nominal growth of 10 per cent plus. An economy growing at 10 per cent automatically creates a tailwind for companies operating in it. Because the Indian economy grows at a high rate, even average companies deliver a 10-12 per cent growth.

In CY2026, the US economy is estimated to grow at 2.3 per cent, Japan at 1 per cent, Germany at 1.1 per cent, 4.7 per cent for China, 1.8 per cent for Brazil, 3.5 per cent for South Korea and so on. For companies in Japan, Germany or South Korea to deliver 12-15 per cent growth, they need to be standout performers in sectors that are growing at 2-3 times the pace of the economy. Or they need to be exporters to other countries.  Export revenues are vulnerable to the trade and tariff policies of the buyer country. All this makes 12-15 per cent growth (and thus wealth creation) harder to come by, when diversifying out of India.
Interest rates

Between January and October 2026, the Brazilian stock market was one of the top gainers in the world with the Bovespa racing by 30 per cent. These gains were driven by foreign investors betting on Brazil as a proxy to the commodities rally, and optimism about its national elections. However, after the October election delivered a surprise result — the incumbent Left-leaning President Lula returned to power — foreign investors have been in pullout mode. This has seen Bovespa tanking  over 20 per cent and the Brazilian Real slipping  16 per cent against the dollar.

The reason for this extreme reaction to election results lies in Brazil’s ultra-high interest rates — its 10-year government bond trades at a 15 per cent yield. The Brazil government’s Budget deficits of 8 per cent plus, combined with high inflation, have prompted Brazil’s central bank to peg its policy rate at 13.75 per cent, setting a very high bar on borrowing costs for companies. Before the elections, expectations were high that Lula would be ousted and replaced by right-leaning Flavio Bolsonaro, who would roll out fiscal reforms and bring down rates. But as election results dashed these hopes, it sparked a capital exodus.

Even without political upheavals though, interest rates in an economy matter to equity investors, because rates decide equity valuations. The PE you should pay for a 10 per cent growth from a US-listed stock when US interest rates are at 5 per cent should be lower than the PE you pay at 2 per cent interest rates.
Currency moves

Driven by foreign investor pullouts, the Indian rupee has weakened significantly against the US dollar and most other global currencies in the last three years. This has led many investors to assume that they are ‘hedging’ against rupee depreciation by investing overseas. But this can cut both ways. Indian investors betting on Brazilian markets this year faced the double-whammy of falling stock prices along with a tanking Real.

Export-oriented countries may like to deliberately weaken their currencies against the dollar, to shore up their competitive edge. If you’re an Indian investor betting on such countries, bouts of currency depreciation are a risk to factor in.

The one currency that has shown steady strength against the rupee over the long term is the US dollar. The USD has, in the long run, gained a predictable 3-4 per cent a year against the INR. However, even there, there can be periods of contrary movement. The sudden return of foreign flows in the past month, for example, has led to the rupee surging from 96.8/USD in early October to 92.6/USD now. This move has wiped out the 4.5 per cent gain Indian investors had made from the US S&P 500 until November.
National priorities

India is a democratic country with a capital market that operates largely on free-market principles. Therefore, corporate fortunes in India largely move in line with how the economy is doing. However, this may not be true of every foreign market.

In the last five years, the Chinese economy has been one of the fastest growing in the world with real GDP growth of 4.5-5.5 per cent. It has also been making great strides in research, automation, AI, robotics and remains the manufacturing powerhouse of the world. Despite all this though, the Chinese stock market has gone nowhere, with the mainland HangSeng Index delivering just a 5 per cent CAGR and the Shanghai CSI 300 a negative return. Ditto for the Hangseng Tech index, which despite housing world-leading tech companies, has sat out the AI bull run.

The reasons have to do with China’s national priorities, which focus on capacity-building and low-cost manufacturing, to drive export growth in any up-and-coming industry. National policies that consistently favour State-backed enterprises and over-capacity have led to poor profitability for the private corporate sector. An extended downcycle in China’s property market has also hit the domestic economy and consumption.

National priorities apart, direct market interventions by State entities are also a factor to consider in some markets. In Japan, the Government Pension Fund and the Bank of Japan buy and sell large volumes of listed stocks and ETFs (exchange traded funds), influencing market direction. Gauging their moves is thus critical to winning in Japanese markets.
Politics, governance

Countries that are subject to regime-changes without the benefit of elections, military coups or civil wars are obviously not great places to do business. Such risks in foreign investing are easier to spot.

However, many foreign investors were taken by surprise at MSCI’s recent announcement that it was considering dropping Indonesia from its emerging market indices. MSCI’s complaint was that market regulators in Indonesia were not doing enough to curb rampant price manipulation and cornering of free float in the large conglomerates that make up the bellwethers of that market. Spotting stock price manipulation can be doubly difficult in foreign markets, where one isn’t aren’t familiar with key players or regulations.

Governance issues, specific to a company, are even harder to sniff out. For Indian investors, the Nvidia stock has been a poster-boy for wealth creation through foreign stocks. But it is only after Nvidia boss Jensen Huang’s extra-marital affairs came to light that the other chinks in the company’s armour have been exposed — whether it is the company’s high dependence on Huang to keep its customer and vendor relationships going, its complex web of buyer financing deals or complete lack of succession planning. Researching the governance and management of companies in your home market is a tough task, doing so for foreign securities can be close to impossible.
Overall, to succeed in equity investing, buying what you know and understand is key. The farther you stray from your home market, the less you can follow this tenet.

title: Global investing isn’t a piece of cake
